discovery.insight_text: The massive capital flooding into autonomous AI agents is hitting a structural adoption ceiling because enterprises lack the tools to measure ROI and the control architectures to safely govern autonomous software actions.

mechanism.description: As AI applications transition from simple copilots to fully autonomous agents (e.g., Metaview's 'fillmore' or IBM Bob), the primary friction for enterprise buyers moves from cognitive performance to governance and observability. If an agent operates independently but its productivity output cannot be measured (Ascerta's focus) and its actions cannot be secured or governed by human-equivalent policy controls (Okta and Equals Money's focus), the enterprise cannot deploy it at scale. This creates a bottleneck migration where the rate of commercial adoption is governed not by model intelligence, but by the maturity of the measurement and compliance integration layers.

UPDATED 16:27 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026
NetApp hands storage operations to AI agents, but humans still draw the boundaries
by Jonathan Anthony
Artificial intelligence is turning nearly every enterprise workload into a data workload, and data governance is becoming the test of whether companies can trust autonomous systems with the infrastructure underneath. The question is no longer only where data lives, but what is allowed to act on it.
Enterprise data now sits across on-premises data centers, public clouds and neoclouds, and storage providers are racing to tie that infrastructure to production AI . Adding another silo is the wrong answer, according to Sandeep Singh (pictured, right), senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp Inc., who calls for one data foundation that behaves the same way everywhere.
"We know that the customers are going to use a variety of locations for the right fit for them," Singh said. "What becomes fundamentally important for customers is to have a consistent data infrastructure strategy that underpins it all so that they can get a consistent set of data capabilities combined with a consistent operational experience across the various environments."
Singh and Helen Yu (left), founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., spoke with theCUBE Research's Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed why consistent data, clear accountability and policy guardrails must come before enterprises hand infrastructure decisions to AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)
Data governance moves into the autonomous control plane
Consistency is not only a technical concern. Yu, who advises companies on AI deployment, sees the bigger gap in how organizations are structured. Teams without trusted data route around official systems, which is how shadow AI and shadow IT take hold, she noted.
"It's not a storage problem. It's a leadership and accountability issue," Yu said. "When teams don't have access to consistent data, trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds."
On the infrastructure side, NetApp pairs a consistent data plane with a unified control plane shared by agents and humans. Its hybrid cloud tools with autonomous controls , delivered through NetApp Console, let customers set policies and boundaries across their fleet while agents keep infrastructure operating within those boundaries. In one keynote demo, agents caught a nighttime performance anomaly instead of paging an engineer, Singh noted.
"Agents can in real time implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there's compliance to the boundary conditions there," Singh said. "And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved and there's no noisy neighbor effect. And there's an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up."
Trust in that model depends on accountability as much as automation. Letting an algorithm decide is not a governance model, according to Yu, who urges leaders to measure automation against business outcomes rather than tasks removed. She extends data governance to machines through the RACI framework: responsible, accountable, consulted and informed.
"Now you need to incorporate the machine or agents into your RACI chart. Who owns what data? Who has access to what data?" Yu said. "And then when you're going to make an exception, who has the right to override the exception?"

UPDATED 16:41 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026
CrowdStrike and CoreWeave bring AI security to machine speed
by Victoria Gayton
AI-native cybersecurity requires defenses that can keep pace with attackers while protecting infrastructure that never stops running. That challenge is bringing security expertise and specialized computing closer together, with automation embedded throughout the systems enterprises use to train and run models.
CrowdStrike's fastest observed eCrime attacker breakout time in 2025 was 27 seconds, underscoring the urgency of faster response, according to Bartley Richardson (pictured, left), chief of AI at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. Meeting that challenge requires computing capacity for both training and inference.
"You can't have humans combat this alone," he said. "You need machine-speed defense, and that relies on critical infrastructure."
Richardson and Jim Higgins (right), chief information security officer of CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research's Dave Vellante and John Furrier at the Fully Connected event , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed machine-speed defense, infrastructure-level security and operational trust. (* Disclosure below.)
Cyber models turn attacks into training data
The partnership combines CrowdStrike's security data and adversary expertise with CoreWeave's infrastructure capabilities. CoreWeave supplies training and inference capacity for SafeMind and serves as a design partner for CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab , according to the company.
"The name of the game ... is adversarial co-evolution, which is a fancy way of saying, 'We train and we steer the best offensive capabilities to attack, to find ways around defensive operations,'" Richardson said. "But then, we train these defensive models on large-scale infrastructure to learn from those attacks."
CoreWeave must strengthen security while keeping its production systems running. That requires integrating protective measures into ongoing operations, according to Higgins.
"That's what I refer to as the aikido of the security problem," he said. "Anything that I can do to affect security while the machine is running and use its own energy to promote the security needs is exactly what I do. Using AI to support and scan my code is incredibly important, but also to be in the [continuous integration and continuous delivery] pipeline to use automation to fix misconfigurations."
AI-native cybersecurity still starts with the basics
Attackers work within budgets and time limits, making the easiest route into an environment an attractive target. Combining several ordinary weaknesses can give them that opening, according to Higgins.
"When you say something is secure, test it and test it often to be sure, but also do the basics," he said. "Patch your stuff and continually test and monitor for those issues."
CrowdStrike is investing in automation to support continuous security operations. Those capabilities must earn the confidence of both CoreWeave and its customers, according to Richardson.
"People ask, 'When do we get to the end of AI?' And I say, 'Never,'" he said. "And then I tell them, 'It's because it's AI until you trust it. Then you start to think of it as automation.' As we make our investment into AI that's always on, what's so important for us is how trust is built into the system."

IBM allows on-prem deployment of its Bob agentic development platform
by Paul Gillin
IBM Corp. today announced a self-hosted deployment option for IBM Bob, its agentic software development platform, allowing enterprises to use artificial intelligence to build and modernize applications within their own infrastructure..
The offering supports on-premises, private-cloud, sovereign-cloud and air-gapped environments. It targets organizations whose sensitive source code, regulated data or critical systems limit their ability to use externally hosted AI development services.
Bob extends AI assistance beyond code generation into software delivery and modernization. IBM said the new deployment option gives customers greater control over data residency, security policies, governance and development workflows.
"Organizations need AI that operates inside environments they have control over, especially when working with sensitive code and regulated data," said Neel Sundaresan, IBM's general manager of AI and automation.
The announcement addresses a recurring obstacle to enterprise AI adoption: applying the technology to applications without moving sensitive information outside approved environments. IBM cited a June report from its Institute for Business Value in which 68% of surveyed executives said meeting data residency and sovereignty requirements across geographies is challenging.
Enterprises can run supported models locally or connect Bob to external model services through hybrid configurations, choosing where AI processing occurs according to each workload's requirements.
In a background post , IBM said the self-hosted option is generally available and retains core Bob capabilities, including its BobShell integrated development environment, parallel tool calling, skills and operating modes. The platform helps developers understand applications, plan changes, carry out development work and validate results.
Customers must provide access to a supported model. For models installed and managed on customers' infrastructure, IBM currently supports Nvidia Corp.'s Nemotron and Poolside Inc.'s Laguna. Hybrid configurations support connections to external model services, giving organizations another option for workloads with different security or operational needs.
IBM said a supported self-hosted model configuration allows source code, development context and build artifacts to remain within the customer-managed environment. Customers can also use eligible existing model investments through a bring-your-own-license arrangement.
The company offered a financial institution as an example, saying developers could use local model processing for core banking software while connecting to an approved external service for less restricted work. Using Bob would ensure that developers retain a consistent experience across those configurations.
Optional premium packages extend Bob to Java modernization and IBM i and IBM Z platforms, subject to licensing and deployment requirements. IBM is positioning the offering for financial services, government, healthcare and critical infrastructure organizations as well as businesses seeking to protect intellectual property.
Investors liked the news. They sent IBM shares up more than 3% in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
